## Brand Strategy
- A "precise design program intended to coordinate all visual communication efforts by the New York Botanical Garden."
- Standards intended as "a framework to coordinate all creative efforts without inhibiting freedom of expression."
- Signed by Howard S. Irwin, President -- urges all staff, consultants, and suppliers to cooperate.
- Exceptions to standards "should be considered only when necessitated by circumstances and then adapted to remain in keeping with the character of this program."

## Logo
- **NYBG abbreviation**: The four-letter abbreviation "NYBG" appears as the primary identifier, set flush left at the top of stationery.
- **Full name**: "The New York Botanical Garden" appears alongside NYBG as the expanded logotype.
- **Seal**: A detailed heraldic/institutional seal showing two figures flanking an oval crest with botanical motifs, dated 1891, with "The New York Botanical Garden" around the perimeter. Used on the cover (green background) and on stationery (small, at bottom of letterhead).
- The seal and the NYBG/logotype appear to serve complementary functions -- the seal for formal/institutional use, the NYBG logotype for everyday communications.

## Typography
- **Primary typeface**: Times Roman -- the "high cost involved in setting type" noted as reason for standardising. Times Roman used because it is "available in any workshop" and "typesetters will satisfy the goal of economy."
  - Times Roman: regular text.
  - Times Roman Italic: emphasis.
  - Times Roman Bold: headings.
  - Full character sets shown for each weight.
- **Display/special typeface**: IBM Selectric Element -- "Large Elite 90" referenced for typewriter-set materials (newsletters, internal communications).
- **Typesetting specifications**: Detailed rules for column widths, leading, word breaks, paragraph indentation, headlines (Times Roman Bold in various point sizes).
- **Newsletter heading**: "The New York Bota[nical Garden]" set in large display type for serial publications like "Botani[cal Garden]" newsletter, using a distinctive large serif treatment.

## Colour
- **Primary colour**: Green -- PMS 347 (the colour on the cover and used throughout signage and stationery). This appears to be the sole brand colour.
- **Stationery**: Printed in green PMS 347.
- **Signage**: White on dark (black/dark green) backgrounds for wayfinding; green accents on identification signs.
- No multi-colour palette defined -- the system is essentially monochrome green plus black/white.

## Graphics / Patterns
- No graphic pattern system. The visual language is purely typographic and signage-based.
- The institutional seal serves as the primary graphic device for formal applications.

## Photography
- Not addressed in this manual.

## Applications
- **Page format system**: Based on DIN (A-series) paper sizes. Proportional relationships shown through geometric construction (golden ratio/root-2 rectangle diagrams). Sizes A0 through A6+ defined with dimensions in mm.
- **Folding**: Standardised folding methods for A3 to smaller sizes.
- **Grid system**: Detailed grid for A4 letterhead -- 3 columns per page, subdivided further. Module = 5 1/16" (31 Picas) x 8 3/4" (53 Picas). Space between columns = 1 Pica. Grids also designed for A5 and other sizes.
- **Stationery**: Letterhead (A4, 7 7/8" x 10 3/4"), continuation sheets, mailing cards (5" x 3 1/8"). Type specs: Times Roman Bold 10 pt for headings, Times Roman Regular 9 pt for address and text.
- **Envelopes**: Regular (#10 standard), air mail (A 1/3rd x 11"), stationery envelopes with return address in green. Multiple formats specified.
- **Botanical publications**: Covers for internal periodicals using the grid system. "Personnel Directory" cover shown.
- **Internal forms**: Grid for tabular forms with specific column/row proportions.
- **Directional signage**: Modular 18" square panels fastened to wooden posts (4" x 4" section). Times Roman Bold, 1 1/2" high type. Arrow/directional indicators. Green on white.
- **Pictographs**: Standard symbols for "One way," "Parking," etc. -- stop signs, no-parking, directional arrows.
- **Outdoor identification signs**: Building and site identification mounted on wood stakes. Green ground with white reversed type.
- **Indoor identification signs**: Plexiglas (1/4" x 6 1/2" square or round), applied to glass surfaces. Room identification includes number, function, and occupant name. Standard restroom/no-smoking pictograms.

## Tone of Voice
- Not formally addressed. The writing throughout is institutional, precise, and utilitarian -- appropriate for a reference manual of this era.

## Outliers / Notable Features
- **Historical artefact**: This is a pre-digital-era graphic standards manual, likely from the early 1990s (seal dated 1891, but the manual itself appears c.1991 based on typography and production methods). It predates desktop publishing becoming standard.
- **DIN format system**: Uncommonly rigorous use of DIN A-series paper standards for a US institution -- suggests European design influence (Vignelli or similar rationalist school).
- **Geometric construction**: The page-size system includes root-2 rectangle and golden ratio diagramming -- a level of mathematical rigour rare in institutional identity manuals.
- **Typewriter specification**: The inclusion of IBM Selectric element specifications reflects the transitional period between typewriter and desktop publishing.
- **Scanned Photoshop PDF**: The document is a scan of a printed manual, exported as image-only PDF via Photoshop -- no searchable text. Text is readable but at limited resolution on some pages.
- **Wayfinding system**: Comprehensive environmental signage for a large outdoor campus (gardens, buildings, parking) with modular panel system.

## Quality Score
**4 / 5** -- An exemplary pre-digital graphic standards manual with exceptional systematic rigour. The DIN format system, geometric construction, comprehensive grid specifications, and modular signage system demonstrate design discipline of the highest order. The typographic specifications are precise and production-ready. Loses a point for the absence of colour palette beyond single green, no photography direction, and no tone of voice -- though these limitations reflect the conventions and scope of institutional manuals of this era. A valuable reference for understanding systematic design methodology.
